title: Kel Kim Corporation v. Central Markets, Inc.
lead: A skating-rink tenant cannot maintain the insurance promised in its lease, but neither impossibility nor the listed force-majeure clause excuses that allocated risk.

actors.name: Kel Kim and its individual guarantors
actors.role: Tenant and guarantors seeking to preserve the lease without the specified coverage.

actors.name: Central Markets and the other landlords
actors.role: Landlords enforcing the insurance requirement and resulting default.

proceedings: Special Term granted the landlords summary judgment, nullified the lease and ordered the tenant to vacate; a divided Appellate Division affirmed.
The Court of Appeals unanimously affirmed with costs on December 21, 1987.
limits: The ruling concerns the lease’s insurance allocation and bounded similar-causes clause. Later procurement of coverage did not alter the affirmed vacatur order.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A former supermarket becomes a skating rink under an insured lease
sections.cue: What coverage did the tenant promise?
paragraphs: In early 1980, Kel Kim leased a vacant supermarket in Clifton Park for ten years with two five-year renewal options. The parties expected a public roller-skating rink, although the lease did not limit use to that business. Kel Kim promised continuous public liability insurance with responsible, solvent insurers: at least $500,000 for one person and $1 million for a single accident in the aggregate.

Kel Kim obtained coverage and operated for six years without incident. In November 1985 its insurer said the policy would expire January 6, 1986 without renewal because a reinsurer’s finances were uncertain under court-appointed administration.

sources.pinpoint: 70 N.Y.2d 901; lease, insurance undertaking and nonrenewal

sections.title: The insurance shortfall produces default and a declaratory suit
sections.cue: What replacement coverage did Kel Kim obtain?
paragraphs: Kel Kim informed the landlords and asserted that exhaustive efforts could not secure replacement limits during the liability-insurance crisis. On January 7, 1986, after expiration left the tenant uninsured, the landlords demanded cure within thirty days or surrender.

A $500,000 aggregate policy became effective March 1, 1986. Kel Kim maintained that no insurer would cover a roller rink above that limit; it finally obtained the required coverage in August 1987. Kel Kim and its individual guarantors sought a declaration excusing the insurance obligation. Special Term instead granted the landlords summary judgment, nullified the lease and ordered vacatur. A divided Appellate Division affirmed.

sections.title: Common-law impossibility does not shift a foreseeable coverage risk
paragraphs: The Court of Appeals stressed the narrowness of excuse doctrines because agreements allocate performance risks. Its impossibility rule required objective impossibility from destruction of the subject matter or means of performance through an event that could neither be foreseen nor guarded against by contract.

Kel Kim expressly undertook procurement and continuous maintenance of the stated coverage. Inability to obtain that insurance was a contingency the parties could foresee and address. The court therefore rejected excuse without needing a universal finding that coverage was always available or accepting every assertion about the market.

sections.title: The force-majeure list does not include this insurance-market event
sections.cue: How did the residual words and final judgment operate?
paragraphs: The clause excused delay from labor disputes, unavailable materials, failed utilities, restrictive laws or regulations, riots, insurrection, war, adverse weather, acts of God and similar uncontrollable causes, for the period of delay. Insurance unavailability was absent. The general similar-causes language stayed bounded by the listed events affecting daily operations, rather than reaching every difficulty beyond control.

Liability insurance protected the landlords’ separate economic interests while the tenant chose to keep operating. That role distinguished it from the listed operational interruptions. On December 21, 1987, the unsigned memorandum affirmed with costs. Chief Judge Wachtler and Judges Simons, Kaye, Alexander, Titone, Hancock and Bellacosa all concurred without separate writing. The result preserved lease nullification and the order to vacate, not merely a damages or arrears award.

sources.pinpoint: 902–903 and sole note; clause construction, disposition and lineup
